description: Our project focuses on developing an interactive Mars mapping tool to support scientific exploration by a human astronaut working alongside a robotic companion. By combining different types of Martian data, we aim to make exploration safer, more efficient, and scientifically valuable. A key priority is protecting the astronaut's health and safety while taking advantage of the complementary capabilities of humans and robots.
summary: ARES-X Mars Navigator is an EVA planner for the first astronauts walking on Mars. It answers one question: is this walk safe, and when should the astronaut go? Our test site is the boxwork ridges on Mount Sharp in Gale Crater, explored by Curiosity in 2025–26. Astronauts would sample those rocks to learn how long groundwater lasted on Mars. The astronaut taps a sample site on a 1 m NASA/USGS terrain map. ARES-X then plans the safest, fastest route and checks it against slope limits, oxygen, cooling water, suit and rover batteries, and daylight. The result is a clear GO or NO-GO. It also simulates the walk: radio links, ridges that block the signal, and position uncertainty without GPS. A relay rover parked on a high point raises the base’s live link from 21% to 100% of the walk. Mars is 4–22 light-minutes from Earth, so crews must plan for themselves. ARES-X gives them a planner built entirely on real Mars data.
details:
ARES-X Mars Navigator is a map app for planning a walk on Mars. We built it around one real site: the boxwork ridges on Mount Sharp in Gale Crater, which Curiosity explored in 2025 and 2026. The map puts a HiRISE colour image on a 1 m elevation model. On top it shows slopes and no-go terrain, Curiosity’s real drive, 81 Navcam photos placed where the rover took them, and a THEMIS thermal-inertia layer that hints at sand versus rock.

The astronaut picks a destination on the map. The app then searches for the fastest route that stays inside our limits: the rover drives on slopes up to 15° and keeps out of the ridges, and the astronaut walks the rest on slopes up to 20°. For that route it works out walking time, metabolic load, oxygen, cooling water and battery use, and adds a safety margin. It then gives a GO or NO-GO, with the best start time for the current Mars season and daylight.

The models come from published work. Walking speed follows Apollo data and drops on slopes. Metabolic rate uses the gravity-corrected Pandolf equation from NASA JSC. Oxygen and cooling water come from a heat balance of the suit. For radio, we check line of sight on the elevation model, including the curvature of Mars. A simulation then plays the walk forward. It shows which radio links are up, when the base is looking at old data, and how the astronaut’s position uncertainty grows, since Mars has no GPS.

The idea we like most is the relay rover. It is an uncrewed rover parked on a high point before the walk starts. ARES-X picks the spot from the planned route, and the crew can still move it by hand. On our test walk it raised the time the base can hear the astronaut from 21% to 100%.

Mars is 4 to 22 light-minutes from Earth, so the crew has to make these decisions without waiting for Mission Control. ARES-X gives them a go/no-go based on real data. It works for any site with an elevation model and imagery, and the same approach could help field teams in remote terrain on Earth.

We wrote it in Python with Streamlit, Folium/Leaflet, rasterio/GDAL, NumPy, SciPy, pandas and scikit-image, and rendered the demo video with HTML5 Canvas. We planned around these limits: a walk of at most 4 hours with a 25% reserve, a 20° walking limit, and a crew that must decide on its own because of the Earth delay. Radiation from one walk is small; a solar particle event is the real danger. The app shows the uncertainty of its results, and every assumption is written down in the project.
